title: Margerison-McCann, Myers-Briggs, Hackman, Katzenbach & Smith
blurb: Know the elements of four more team models and explain how a project manager would use each one.
question: A council's housing-repairs system is being delivered by department leads who meet monthly, report only on their own areas and keep hitting data errors and blocked access to tenant records. How could the project manager use Margerison-McCann, Myers-Briggs, Hackman and Katzenbach and Smith to diagnose and improve the team?

teach.body: Each model looks at a team from a different angle. MARGERISON-McCANN: which types of WORK does the team need covered, and who prefers each? MYERS-BRIGGS (MBTI): how do INDIVIDUALS prefer to take in information, decide and relate? HACKMAN: what CONDITIONS make team success more likely? KATZENBACH AND SMITH: how far has this group travelled from a working group towards a high-performing team? A project manager picks the lens that fits the problem in front of them.

teach.caption: Read clockwise from the top: Reporter-Adviser, Creator-Innovator, Explorer-Promoter, Assessor-Developer, Thruster-Organiser, Concluder-Producer, Controller-Inspector, Upholder-Maintainer. Linking sits at the hub.

teach.body: The wheel shows eight types of work every team must do, from advising and innovating through to inspecting and maintaining. Each person's work preferences place them in a sector of the wheel. LINKING sits at the centre: co-ordinating and integrating everyone's work, a skill all members need and the leader needs most. The PM uses it to check every sector is covered, match work to preferences and spot gaps, such as no Controller-Inspector checking detail.

head: Pair
Question
The two preferences
rows: Extraversion: people and action. Introversion: inner ideas
How do you take in information?
Sensing: facts and detail. iNtuition: patterns, possibilities
Thinking: logic, criteria. Feeling: values, effect on people
How do you approach the outer world?
Judging: planned, decided. Perceiving: flexible, open
teach.caption: One preference from each pair gives 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 types, such as ISTJ or ENFP. They are preferences, not abilities, and no type is better. Use MBTI for self-awareness and communication, not for selection or promotion.

root.label: Team success more likely when there is…

children.label: Enabling structure
children.sub: good task design, right size and mix, norms

teach.caption: Hackman's point: leaders can't make a team great by force of personality. They create the conditions, then coach at the start (motivation), midpoint (strategy) and end (learning).

teach.h: Katzenbach and Smith's team performance curve
teach.caption: Working group → pseudo-team → potential team → real team → high-performing team. The pseudo-team dips BELOW a working group: it calls itself a team but has no shared goal or mutual accountability.

teach.h: Katzenbach and Smith: what makes a real team
teach.body: A REAL team is a small number of people with complementary skills, committed to a common purpose, performance goals and approach, for which they hold themselves mutually accountable. A WORKING GROUP just shares information; each member is judged on their own output, and that can be fine. A POTENTIAL team is trying but lacks clarity or accountability. A HIGH-PERFORMING team adds deep commitment to each other's growth. The PM uses the curve to decide whether a real team is needed, then builds the missing ingredients.

Katzenbach and Smith: the department leads are a working group, but integration work is interdependent, so the PM builds shared goals and mutual accountability. Hackman: the team can't reach tenant data (weak supportive context), so the PM asks the sponsor to unblock access. Margerison-McCann: nobody prefers Controller-Inspector work, which explains the data errors, so checking is assigned. MBTI: a short workshop helps Thinking-led engineers and Feeling-led housing officers understand each other.

teach.text: Keep the numbers straight: Belbin has 9 roles, Margerison-McCann has 8 roles plus the Linker at the centre, MBTI has 4 preference pairs giving 16 types, Hackman has 5 conditions and Katzenbach and Smith have 5 points on the curve. Hackman's conditions are not stages, and the pseudo-team is the WORST performer on the curve, below a working group.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the model and state its elements accurately (roles, preferences, conditions or curve points).
Say what it tells the PM: work coverage, individual preferences, missing conditions or team maturity.
Apply it to the scenario: which gap or stage does the evidence point to?
State the action the PM would take, such as reallocating work or fixing a missing condition.
Add a limitation: models describe preferences or conditions, so don't use them to label or select people.
Margerison-McCann: 8 work-preference roles around the central Linker; check all types of work are covered.
Myers-Briggs: E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P give 16 types; preferences, not abilities; not for selection.
Hackman: real team, compelling direction, enabling structure, supportive context, expert coaching.
Katzenbach and Smith: working group, pseudo-team, potential team, real team, high-performing team.
A real team: small, complementary skills, common purpose, goals and approach, mutual accountability.

summary: You can now state the elements of the Margerison-McCann wheel, Myers-Briggs, Hackman's conditions and Katzenbach and Smith's performance curve. You can also explain how a project manager would use each one to diagnose and improve a team, and the limits of each.

A.q: In the Margerison-McCann Team Management Wheel, which role sits at the centre?
A.why: Linking sits at the hub of the wheel: co-ordinating and integrating the work of the eight sectors around it.

whyNot.0: Thruster-Organiser is one of the eight roles around the wheel, focused on organising.
whyNot.2: Reporter-Adviser is one of the eight outer roles, focused on advising.
whyNot.3: Co-ordinator is a Belbin people role, not part of the Margerison-McCann wheel.

A.q: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator combines four preference pairs into how many personality types?
A.why: Choosing one preference from each of the four pairs gives 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 types.

whyNot.0: Four is the number of preference pairs, not the number of types.
whyNot.1: Eight is the number of outer roles on the Margerison-McCann wheel.
whyNot.2: Nine is the number of Belbin team roles.

A.q: Which of the following is one of Hackman's conditions for team effectiveness?
A.why: A compelling direction (a clear, challenging and consequential purpose) is one of Hackman's five conditions.

whyNot.0: Hackman argued that conditions, not the leader's personality, make team success more likely.
whyNot.1: Hackman favoured the right size and mix (an enabling structure); bigger is not better.
whyNot.3: Rewards form part of a supportive context, but a bonus scheme on its own isn't one of the five conditions.

B.q: On Katzenbach and Smith's team performance curve, which kind of group delivers the LOWEST performance impact?
B.why: A pseudo-team calls itself a team but has no common purpose or mutual accountability, so it performs below even a working group.

whyNot.1: A working group performs at the baseline: members share information and deliver their own work.
whyNot.2: A potential team is trying to improve and performs above a working group.
whyNot.3: A real team performs well above both, thanks to mutual accountability.

B.q: A team's contracts and data returns keep going out with errors. Using the Team Management Wheel, which work preference is most needed?
B.why: The Controller-Inspector prefers inspecting work: checking detail, accuracy and compliance with standards.

whyNot.0: The Explorer-Promoter looks outward for opportunities and promotes ideas, not detailed checking.
whyNot.1: The Creator-Innovator generates new ideas rather than checking accuracy.
whyNot.3: The Thruster-Organiser makes things happen to deadlines, not detailed inspection.

B.q: Which Myers-Briggs preference pair describes how a person prefers to make decisions?
B.why: Thinking and Feeling describe decision-making: logic and objective criteria versus values and the effect on people.

whyNot.0: Extraversion and Introversion describe where a person focuses their energy.
whyNot.1: Sensing and Intuition describe how a person takes in information.
whyNot.2: Judging and Perceiving describe how a person approaches the outer world: planned or flexible.

C.q: A capable team has a clear, stretching goal but keeps stalling because it can't get timely data from other departments and has no budget for test equipment. Which of Hackman's conditions is weakest?
C.why: A supportive context means the organisation provides information, resources, training and rewards. Missing data and equipment are context failures.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests unclear boundaries or unstable membership.
whyNot.1: The goal is clear and stretching, so direction is strong.
whyNot.2: Enabling structure concerns task design, team size and mix, and norms, none of which is the problem here.

C.q: Five regional managers meet monthly to share updates and are each judged only on their own region. The sponsor wants them 'turned into a team'. Using Katzenbach and Smith, what is the BEST advice?
options: A working group: build a team only if joint goals need it
A pseudo-team: disband it and let managers work alone
A real team: add more meetings to raise performance
A potential team: make one manager accountable for all
C.why: They are a working group, which is fine when results are the sum of individual efforts. A real team is worth building only if there is a shared goal that needs mutual accountability.

whyNot.1: They don't claim a collective purpose, so they aren't a pseudo-team, and disbanding them loses useful sharing.
whyNot.2: Without common goals and mutual accountability they are not a real team, and more meetings won't make them one.
whyNot.3: Making one person accountable is the opposite of the MUTUAL accountability a real team needs.

C.q: A project manager plans to use team members' Myers-Briggs types to decide who is promoted to workstream lead. Why is this inappropriate?
options: Types must be scored by the sponsor
C.why: MBTI describes preferences, not competence or performance, and no type is better than another, so it should not drive selection or promotion.

whyNot.0: Preferences are seen as fairly stable; the issue is that they don't measure ability.
whyNot.2: MBTI covers both extraverted and introverted preferences equally.
whyNot.3: MBTI is a self-report questionnaire; the sponsor has no scoring role.

reteach.title: Think of it like a restaurant kitchen
reteach.question: Picture a busy restaurant kitchen. How would each of the four models help the head chef understand and improve the brigade?

blocks.body: MARGERISON-McCANN: is every type of work covered? Someone dreams up dishes, someone orders stock, someone plates up, someone checks hygiene, and the head chef links it all. MBTI: why does one chef want the menu fixed a week ahead while another loves improvising? HACKMAN: are the conditions right: a clear goal, a sensible layout, enough knives and a mentor on hand? KATZENBACH AND SMITH: are the cooks just working side by side, or do they own each service together?

rows.label: Myers-Briggs
values: How does each cook prefer to work?

rows.label: Hackman
values: Does the kitchen set us up to win?

rows.label: Katzenbach & Smith
values: Are we a real team yet?

blocks.text: The head chef is the Linker on the wheel, but on Katzenbach and Smith's curve every cook shares accountability. A single person being answerable for everything is a sign of a working group, not a real team.

explain.body: Eight types of team work (advising, innovating, promoting, developing, organising, producing, inspecting, maintaining) each match a work-preference role on the wheel. Linking, at the centre, co-ordinates them all. Everyone needs linking skills; the leader needs them most.

test.q: In the Team Management Wheel, which set of skills does Margerison-McCann say every member needs, and the leader most of all?
test.why: Linking (co-ordinating and integrating the team's work) sits at the centre and is needed by everyone, especially the leader.

whyNot.0: Promoting is the work type of the Explorer-Promoter sector.
whyNot.1: Inspecting is the work type of the Controller-Inspector sector.
whyNot.3: Maintaining is the work type of the Upholder-Maintainer sector.

explain.body: Four pairs: Extraversion/Introversion (energy), Sensing/iNtuition (information), Thinking/Feeling (decisions), Judging/Perceiving (structure versus flexibility). One from each gives 16 types. Use it to improve self-awareness, communication and understanding, never to rank or select people.

letters.sub: people and action, or inner ideas

test.q: A team member likes clear plans, early decisions and getting things closed off. Which Myers-Briggs preference does this suggest?
test.why: A Judging preference favours structure, planning and reaching closure.

whyNot.0: Perceiving favours flexibility and keeping options open, the opposite preference.
whyNot.2: Sensing is about taking in concrete facts and detail, not about closure.
whyNot.3: Feeling is about deciding by values and the effect on people.

explain.body: Five conditions make team success more likely: a real team, a compelling direction, an enabling structure, a supportive context and expert coaching. The leader's job is to create and protect these conditions, then coach at the right moments.

test.q: Which statement best describes Hackman's model?
options: Five conditions that make success likely
Five stages all teams pass through
Five personality types a team needs
Five points on a performance curve
test.why: Hackman set out five conditions that make team effectiveness more likely, rather than stages, types or a curve.

whyNot.1: Stages that teams pass through describe Tuckman's model.
whyNot.2: Hackman doesn't classify personalities; that is closer to MBTI.
whyNot.3: The five-point performance curve is Katzenbach and Smith's.

explain.body: The curve runs working group, pseudo-team, potential team, real team, high-performing team. What tips a group into a real team is a common purpose, goals and approach with MUTUAL accountability, among a small number of people with complementary skills.

steps.label: Pseudo-team
steps.sub: Calls itself a team; no shared goal

steps.label: High-performing
steps.sub: Also committed to each other's growth

test.q: According to Katzenbach and Smith, which feature most distinguishes a REAL team from a working group?
options: All members report to one manager
A large number of skilled people
test.why: Real teams hold themselves mutually accountable for a common purpose and goals; working group members are accountable only for their own work.

whyNot.0: Reporting lines don't create a team; working groups often share a manager.
whyNot.1: Sharing updates is exactly what a working group does.
whyNot.2: Katzenbach and Smith describe a real team as a SMALL number of people.
